questions.problem:
Given that $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $C,$ find $⟨a,\,b-(1+3\text{i})c⟩$ if 

$\,$ $⟨b,a⟩=1+\text{i}\,$ and $\,⟨a,c⟩=2.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. 

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is antilinear in the second argument:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨a,\,b-(1+3\text{i})c⟩ & =⟨a,b⟩-⟨a,(1+3\text{i})c⟩ \\  & =⟨a,b⟩-(\overset{―}{1+3\text{i}})⟨a,c⟩ \\  & =⟨a,b⟩-(1-3\text{i})⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨a,b⟩-(1-3\text{i})⟨a,c⟩ & =\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}-(1-3\text{i})⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute the values for $⟨b,a⟩$ and $⟨a,c⟩:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}-(1-3\text{i})⟨a,c⟩ & =\overset{―}{1+\text{i}}-(1-3\text{i})\cdot 2 \\  & =1-\text{i}-2+6\text{i} \\  & =-1+5\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Given that $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ is the standard Hermitian inner product over $C,$ find $⟨a,\,(4-\text{i})b+c⟩$ if  

$\,$ $⟨b,a⟩=-1-\text{i}\,$ and $\,⟨a,c⟩=5.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties. 

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

First, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ is antilinear in the second argument:

$$
\begin{aligned}⟨a,\,(4-\text{i})b+c⟩ & =⟨a,(4-\text{i})b⟩+⟨a,c⟩ \\  & =(\overset{―}{4-\text{i}})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩ \\  & =(4+\text{i})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that the inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry:

$$
\begin{aligned}(4+\text{i})⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c\text{ }⟩ & =(4+\text{i})\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+⟨a,c⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we substitute the values for $⟨b,a⟩$ and $⟨a,c⟩:$  

$$
\begin{aligned}(4+\text{i})\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}+⟨a,c⟩ & =(4+\text{i})\cdot (\overset{―}{-1-\text{i}})+5 \\  & =(4+\text{i})\cdot (-1+\text{i})+5 \\  & =-5+3\text{i}+5 \\  & =3\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ 
Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $⟨a,a⟩\in R$ for any $a\in {C}^{n}$

II. $⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C$

III. $⟨a,b⟩=⟨b,a⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$  $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number.

- Statement II is false. To factor out a constant multiple from the second argument, we must change it to its complex conjugate.

- Statement III is false. The inner product over $C$ has conjugate symmetry.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."

questions.problem:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ 
Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨a,b⟩}$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$

II. $i⟨a,b⟩=⟨a,-ib⟩$ for any  $a,b\in {C}^{n}$

III. There is vector $a\in {C}^{n}$ such that  $⟨a,a⟩<0$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is false. A complex number is equal to its conjugate if and only if it is a real number. The inner product over $C$  is a complex number in general.

- Statement II is true. Indeed, by the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument, we have 

$$
⟨a,-ib⟩=\overset{―}{(-i)}⟨a,b⟩=i⟨a,b⟩.
$$

- Statement III is false.  The inner product over $C$ is positive-definite. So, for any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have
$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩\ge 0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "II only."

questions.problem:
Consider the standard Hermitian inner product $⟨\,\cdot \,,\,\cdot \,⟩$ over $C.$ 
Which of the following statements are true? 

I. $⟨ia,b⟩=i⟨a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$

II. $⟨a,\overset{―}{\alpha }b⟩=⟨\alpha a,b⟩$ for any $a,b\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C$

III. $⟨ia,a⟩\in R$ for any $a\in {C}^{n}$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that the standard Hermitian inner product over $C$ satisfies the following properties:

- It is linear in the first argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a+b,c⟩=⟨a,c⟩+⟨b,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨\alpha a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩.$

- It is antilinear in the second argument. For any $a,b,c\in {C}^{n}$ and any $\alpha \in C,$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b+c⟩=⟨a,b⟩+⟨a,c⟩\,$ and $\,⟨a,\alpha b⟩=\overset{―}{\alpha }⟨a,b⟩.$

- It has conjugate symmetry. For any $a,b\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,b⟩=\overset{―}{⟨b,a⟩}.$

- It is positive-definite. For any $a\in {C}^{n},$ we have

$\,$ $⟨a,a⟩$ is a non-negative real number, and $⟨a,a⟩=0$ if and only if $a=0.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements. 

- Statement I is true.  Indeed, the inner product in ${C}^{n}$ is linear in the first argument. So, a constant multiple from the first argument can be factored out.

- Statement II is true. By the antilinearity of a complex inner product in the second argument and linearity in the first argument, we have 

$$
⟨a,\overset{―}{\alpha }b⟩=\overset{―}{(\overset{―}{\alpha })}⟨a,b⟩=\alpha ⟨a,b⟩=⟨\alpha a,b⟩.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that $⟨a,a⟩\in R$ for any $a\in {C}^{n}.$ Therefore, if $a\ne 0,$ then

$$
⟨ia,a⟩=i⟨a,a⟩\notin R.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."
